doc.title: Jon Hendricks — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Singing in Detroit with Jesse Juice Jones
summary: He sang popular jazz tunes like Nagasaki with his hard-drinking brother-in-law, and admits poor sense of dates.

story.theme_name: First paying gigs: getting started as a young professional
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: Yes it is. This is something I know very little about, but it intrigues me: after high school, you lived in Detroit and sang with your brother-in-law. Is it Jesse Jones?

Jesse Jones. They called him Juice Jones for obvious reasons. I almost never saw him sober. He was a drinker. In those days, that was the dope of choice, alcohol. Alcohol should be proscribed as a narcotic, incidentally. They’re very loathe to do that, because the liquor companies spend a lot of money lobbying, but that stuff should be proscribed as a narcotic, because it’s caused the death of so many people and so many great artists, and it’s completely useless. It has no real use.
A mind-changing substance. What did you perform with Juice Jones?
I performed whatever were the popular jazz songs of the day, like Nagasaki. Have you ever heard that?

[Hendricks sings:] “Hot ginger and dynamite. That’s all they serve at night. Back in Nagasaki where the fellers chew tobaccy and the women wicky wacky woo.” That was a big hit I think for Cab Calloway. He did that. It was a great song.
Let me see. I’m bad chronologically. I’m very, very bad, because I never think in terms of time and years.
To me it’s 1937 right now. There’s no difference in my mind in time. But it was about ’35. ’36, I think. ’36 would be nearer.
